mcqs.question: A table is partitioned by order_date. A query filters WHERE order_date = '2024-06-01'. How does partition pruning cut cost compared to predicate pushdown alone?
options: It can skip entire partitions at the metadata/catalog level, often without listing the files inside non-matching partitions at all
It works identically to predicate pushdown, just with a different name
It only works if the table has fewer than 100 rows
It requires reading every partition's files to check their contents first
mcqs.explanation: Partition pruning operates at the catalog/metadata level, eliminating entire non-matching partitions before even listing their files — a coarser, cheaper elimination than per-row-group stats checking. It's a distinct mechanism from predicate pushdown, has no row-count minimum, and specifically avoids reading non-matching partitions' files.

mcqs.question: A table is partitioned by date, and a query also filters by customer_region within a single day's partition. What does clustering by customer_region add on top of the date partitioning?
options: It creates a separate partition for each region within each date
It physically sorts/groups rows by customer_region within each partition's files, so a region filter has narrow, distinct min/max ranges to prune against via predicate pushdown
It replaces the need for date partitioning entirely
It has no effect unless customer_region is also the partition key
mcqs.explanation: Clustering orders data within a partition so a secondary filter benefits from tight, distinct min/max ranges at the file level — exactly what predicate pushdown needs to be effective, without creating additional partitions. It doesn't create new partitions, doesn't replace the primary partition key, and works precisely because it's independent of the partition key.

mcqs.question: A table is partitioned by event_date. A query filters WHERE EXTRACT(MONTH FROM event_date) = 6 instead of a direct range on event_date. Why does this often scan every partition anyway?
options: Wrapping the partition column in an expression often prevents the engine from determining which partitions could match, so it falls back to scanning all of them
This query is syntactically invalid and will fail
EXTRACT always forces a full table scan regardless of partitioning
The query engine automatically rewrites this into a direct partition filter
mcqs.explanation: Many query planners can't evaluate an expression like EXTRACT against partition boundaries to determine which partitions could match, so they conservatively scan everything rather than risk missing a match. The query is valid SQL, EXTRACT itself doesn't force a full scan in every context, and most engines don't automatically rewrite this into a prunable form.

mcqs.question: A table partitioned by (date, hour, customer_id) ends up with thousands of tiny partitions. What's the resulting cost, and why?
options: No cost — more partitions always mean strictly better query performance
The table becomes permanently read-only
Metadata bookkeeping overhead (listing files, tracking partition stats) can exceed the time saved reading data, especially for queries spanning many partitions
This only affects storage cost, never query performance
mcqs.explanation: Every partition, regardless of size, carries metadata overhead the engine must track and consult — with enough tiny partitions, that bookkeeping cost can exceed the benefit of finer pruning, especially for broad queries touching many partitions. More partitions isn't strictly better, tables don't become read-only from partition count, and this directly affects query performance, not just storage.

mcqs.question: A table is almost always queried by date, but a team partitions it by customer_region instead because it 'feels like' a natural business dimension. What's the likely consequence?
options: No consequence, since any partition key provides equal pruning benefit
The table will automatically re-partition itself by date over time
This only matters if the table has more than a million rows
Date-range queries, the dominant access pattern, get none of partitioning's pruning benefit, since the partition key doesn't match how queries actually filter
mcqs.explanation: Partitioning only helps when the key matches actual query filters — choosing a key based on a business dimension rather than real query patterns means the dominant date-range queries can't benefit from partition pruning at all. Partition keys aren't equally effective regardless of choice, tables don't self-repartition, and the mismatch matters regardless of table size.

mcqs.question: How does storage-layer partitioning differ from compute-layer shuffle partitioning, despite sharing the same word?
options: They're actually the same mechanism, just described differently by different teams
Storage partitioning is a persistent, on-disk table property; shuffle partitioning is a transient, per-query runtime decision about redistributing data across workers during execution
Shuffle partitioning only applies to tables that are also storage-partitioned
Storage partition count directly determines the number of shuffle partitions a query will use
mcqs.explanation: These are genuinely different mechanisms at different layers — one is a persistent physical layout decision, the other a transient execution-time data movement decision — that happen to share terminology. They aren't the same mechanism, shuffle partitioning applies regardless of a table's storage partitioning, and there's no direct numeric relationship between the two.
